final_message:
All three versions are written and pass every sample.

**Algorithm (shared):** Each walker is independent. Only the top two bits of the SplitMix64 output are needed, and the final `z ^ (z >> 31)` cannot affect those bits, so all versions skip it. Walkers are split into contiguous ranges over `WORKERS` threads/processes; partial aggregates merge with farthest-tie going to the smallest index, so output is independent of `WORKERS`.

**[Rust `main.rs`](C:/Users/sandh/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions/wonder-full/walkers/rust/src/main.rs):** Rayon pool sized to `WORKERS`. Walker stepping is branchless (offset coordinates, one unsigned compare per axis), since branches on random directions mispredict. Walkers run in interleaved groups of up to 4 per thread so the CPU overlaps the latency-bound SplitMix64 multiply chains; group size shrinks so there are at least as many chunks as workers. Fat LTO and `codegen-units = 1` in [Cargo.toml](C:/Users/sandh/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions/wonder-full/walkers/rust/Cargo.toml).

**[plain.py](C:/Users/sandh/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions/wonder-full/walkers/plain.py):** Standard `multiprocessing` (spawn) over walker ranges for large inputs. For long walks, directions are generated 1024 steps at a time with a single big integer (SWAR): each 64-bit state lives in a 128-bit lane, so big-int add/multiply/mask perform the whole SplitMix64 mixing lane-wise in C; directions are read out through `bytes` and the walk itself is a tight scalar loop. Short walks use a plain scalar loop.

**[fast.py](C:/Users/sandh/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions/wonder-full/walkers/fast.py):** NumPy per walker: all states `seed_j + k·GOLD` are mixed vectorially in `uint64`, then the bounded walk is recovered from the unbounded cumsum via one-sided reflections (blocked cumulative max/min), with a scalar fallback if the walk flips boundaries too often. Paths use int32 when safe. Workers are threads (NumPy releases the GIL here; processes were slower because each pays a Python+NumPy import), except narrow-box/huge inputs where the scalar fallback makes processes worthwhile.

**Results:** All three pass s1a, s1b, s2 and s3 at WORKERS = 1, 2, 3, 16, and agree with each other on extra edge inputs (L=0, B=1 with 100k steps, max seed, odd J). On a benchmark-size input (64×500k, B=300), observed times were Rust ≈0.04s, fast.py ≈1.2s, plain.py ≈1.8s at 16 workers (machine was shared, so timings are indicative).

request.prompt:
You are writing three versions of the same program, one in Rust and two in Python, for a comparison of how
fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Write these three files:

1. `rust/src/main.rs`: Rust, compiled with rustc 1.99 (edition 2024). The Cargo project in `rust/` is set
   up. The only crates you may use are serde (with derive), serde_json, regex and rayon. They are already
   listed in `rust/Cargo.toml` and vendored, so build offline with `cargo build --release --offline` inside
   `rust/`. Do not add other dependencies. You may change the `[profile.release]` settings in
   `rust/Cargo.toml`.
2. `plain.py`: Python 3.13, standard library only.
3. `fast.py`: Python 3.13, standard library plus NumPy 2.2.

Each program is run with the path of one input file as its argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments). It reads that file and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes. The
Python versions are run as `C:\Python313\python.exe plain.py INPUT_PATH` and
`C:\Python313\python.exe fast.py INPUT_PATH`, and the Rust version as the release binary
`rust/target/release/solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Test all three versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside this
folder, and take at most about 45 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time:
never stop a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example
`taskkill /IM python.exe` or `Stop-Process -Name python`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
